extracted.intended_audience: political writers, pamphleteers, critics, and informed readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating political/polemic essays and public‑life critiques, emphasizing factual accuracy, logical causation, use of evidence, and the moral character of public actors. Applicable to writers who marshal statistics, historical examples, and policy arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of facts and arithmetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments must be supported by correct facts and computations; arithmetic or factual errors fatally weaken a case (the author points out many numerical miscalculations, e.g., miscomputed premiums and wrongly cast figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check all sums, dates, and figures against primary sources; minor numeric errors can undermine credibility. Examples in the text show premiums and annuity computations miscast and exports figures wrongly tallied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect temporal order before claiming causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attribute effects to causes whose timing makes such attribution impossible (e.g., an order signed in November could not affect the preceding year's exports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the dates when measures became effective and compare them to the period allegedly affected; ensure the temporal mechanism is plausible before asserting causal links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative explanations and confounders
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid single‑cause explanations for complex phenomena; the text lists multiple plausible causes for trade changes (war conquests altering markets, temporary influxes of cash, merchants' reactions to debts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerate and weigh other plausible factors, show why one factor is more likely than others, and avoid cherry‑picking a convenient cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overgeneralizing from short or single‑year data
rubrics_metrics.description: Single‑year fluctuations are unreliable bases for sweeping conclusions; the author contrasts single‑year drops with multi‑year averages showing trade recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer multi‑year comparisons, averages, or medium balances to measure trends; note that one anomalous year should not be used to prove long‑term decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not build hypotheses on false or unverified premises
rubrics_metrics.description: If an asserted fact is false (e.g., wrong date of an order), any inference drawn from it is unsound; the critic stresses that the author's hypothesis is invalid when founded on a false premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify key premises before reasoning from them; if a foundational fact is uncertain, qualify conclusions or refrain from strong claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion conclusions to the weight of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Small numerical differences or ambiguous data should not be used to justify large or sensational claims (the critic mocks drawing vast inferences from an £80 difference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale the strength of your conclusions to the magnitude and clarity of the data; explicitly acknowledge uncertainty or small effect sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authentic primary sources and transparent citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Support claims with documentary evidence (custom‑house entries, accounts, printed conventions) and cite pages or documents so readers can verify the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote or reference original records and provide precise citations (page numbers, official returns) rather than vague allusions; this increases authority and allows independent checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish rhetorical flourish from demonstrated argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetorical declamation or plausible phrasing cannot substitute for factual demonstration; the critic repeatedly faults the author's 'plausible' but hollow pretences and overblown insinuations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep rhetoric subordinate to evidence: state claims plainly, then support them with verifiable reasoning; avoid letting elegant phrasing mask weak foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to procedural and legal detail when it matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural specifics (when an act or order is signed, when regulations come into force) can crucially affect whether a policy could have caused a given outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing about legal or administrative effects, check enactment dates, provisos, and the statutory timeline; quote the operative provision if necessary to make or refute causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize integrity and consistency in public life
rubrics_metrics.description: Political virtue and steadiness of character in public men are presented as remedies for disorder: uniformity and consistency of character in leaders restore confidence and subordination on esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating public actors or prescriptions for governance, consider moral criteria (consistency, public spirit, integrity) alongside technical policy arguments; argue how character affects institutional outcomes.
